phy-cns-446.why: Cutaneous thermoreceptors detect warming or cooling at free sensory nerve endings. Their signals travel in thinly myelinated A-delta fibres and unmyelinated C fibres, with different populations responding to different temperature ranges.

notes.A: Warm and cool receptors are active during ordinary temperature changes before temperatures become painful.
notes.B: Many cutaneous thermoreceptors have endings in superficial skin, where they can detect changes near the body surface.
notes.C: Innocuous warm and cool sensation is distinct from pain evoked by noxious temperatures, though some sensory fibres respond to both kinds of stimulus.
notes.E: The list includes inaccurate restrictions on stimulus intensity and location and incorrectly classifies all thermoreceptors as nociceptors.

phy-cns-447.why: Most body heat ultimately comes from cellular metabolism. Energy released during cellular respiration can support ATP production and other processes, and much of it is ultimately released as heat.

notes.B: Conduction is transfer of heat between surfaces in contact. It does not generate metabolic heat.
notes.C: Convection carries heat away from skin when surrounding air or water is cooler. It is a transfer mechanism rather than an internal heat source.
notes.D: Evaporation requires energy to turn water into vapour. This takes heat from the body surface.
notes.E: Shivering increases heat production by speeding metabolism in contracting skeletal muscle. It is a specialised response rather than the general source of body heat.

phy-cns-448.why: In the cold, sympathetic vasoconstriction decreases skin blood flow. Less warm blood reaches the surface, so less heat is transferred from the core to the surroundings.

notes.A: Cutaneous vasodilation increases heat delivery to the surface and usually promotes heat loss when the environment is cooler.
notes.B: Increasing metabolic rate produces additional heat. Conserving heat refers to decreasing loss of heat already in the body.
notes.D: Sweat evaporation removes heat and is usually reduced when the body needs to conserve heat.
notes.E: Convection can transfer heat from skin to cooler air or water. Increasing this loss cools rather than conserves heat.

phy-cns-449.why: Hypothalamic circuits, particularly in the preoptic region, integrate core and skin temperature signals. Their outputs adjust sweating, skin blood flow, heat production and temperature-related behaviour.

notes.A: The cortex supports conscious thermal perception and behavioural responses. The main autonomic integration occurs in the hypothalamus.
notes.B: Blood transports heat and skin vessels act as effectors. The vascular system is not the main neural centre for regulation.
notes.C: The septal region participates in limbic circuits. It is not the principal site that integrates thermal signals and coordinates autonomic responses.
notes.D: The amygdala can influence autonomic and behavioural responses to emotion, while the hypothalamus chiefly integrates thermoregulatory signals.

phy-cns-450.why: A central body temperature near 37 °C is typical in healthy adults. It varies with the measurement site, time of day and individual, making 36.9 °C a reasonable representative value.

notes.A: A core temperature of 81.1 °C is incompatible with ordinary human physiology and far above normal.
notes.C: The familiar value 98.6 refers to degrees Fahrenheit and is equivalent to 37 °C, not 98.6 °C.
notes.D: A core temperature of 21.7 °C would represent profound hypothermia rather than a normal adult value.
notes.E: A core temperature near 39.5 °C is elevated and can occur with high fever or hyperthermia.

phy-cns-453.why: As air and surrounding surfaces approach skin temperature, dry heat loss becomes less effective. Evaporation of sweat then accounts for more heat loss, provided humidity and airflow allow the water to evaporate.

notes.A: Radiant heat loss decreases as surrounding surfaces become warmer relative to the skin. Net radiant heat gain is possible.
notes.B: Convective heat loss falls as air temperature approaches skin temperature and can reverse when the air is hotter than skin.
notes.C: Conduction transfers heat to cooler surfaces in contact with the skin. It does not automatically increase as surroundings warm.
notes.E: Evaporation provides a route for cooling even when the air is as warm as or warmer than the skin.

phy-cns-454.why: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, an oily mixture of lipids that commonly enters hair follicles. Sebum spreads over the skin and hair and helps maintain their surface barrier.

notes.A: Adrenaline is a catecholamine released principally by the adrenal medulla, rather than a component of sebum.
notes.C: Saliva is produced by major and minor salivary glands lining or opening into the mouth.
notes.D: Sweat is produced by sweat glands. Eccrine secretion is especially important for evaporative cooling.
notes.E: Mucus is produced by mucous epithelial cells and glands. Sebaceous glands supply a lipid-rich secretion.

phy-cns-455.why: Heat acclimatisation typically causes sweating to begin earlier for a given thermal load and increases sweating capacity. Sweat usually becomes more dilute, allowing more evaporative cooling with less salt loss per unit of sweat.

notes.A: Basal metabolic rate is not ordinarily increased as the principal adaptation for shedding heat. Producing more heat would increase the thermal load.
notes.B: Radiation and convection depend on the gradient between skin and surroundings. Acclimatisation does not ensure that this gradient increases in a hot climate.
notes.C: Heat stress and sweating can trigger fluid conservation rather than a consistent rise in urine output.
notes.E: Increased skin perfusion helps transfer heat from the core. The more characteristic acclimatisation change is better evaporative cooling through sweating.

phy-cns-457.why: Normal thermal control defends a core temperature near 37 °C through coordinated responses. The thresholds for individual sweating, vasodilation and cold-defence responses vary with time of day, measurement and physiological state.

notes.A: A core temperature of 34 °C is hypothermic and would usually activate cold-defence responses.
notes.C: Twenty degrees Celsius is closer to some indoor air temperatures and is far below the normal regulated core temperature.
notes.D: A measurement near 36.3 °C can be normal at some times or sites, but it is below the usual central teaching estimate.
notes.E: A core temperature of 30 °C is markedly hypothermic rather than a normal reference for hypothalamic control.

phy-cns-459.why: The preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus plays a central role in integrating temperature signals and initiating temperature-defence responses. Its downstream pathways adjust heat loss and heat production.

notes.B: Skin thermoreceptors report local warmth or cold. They are sensors rather than the central site for integrating thermal responses.
notes.C: The spinal cord conveys thermal signals and sympathetic commands. It does not contain the main central integrating region.
notes.D: Posterior hypothalamic regions contribute to cold-defence outputs. The classic integration site for thermal input is the preoptic anterior hypothalamus.
notes.E: Brown adipose tissue generates heat when activated. It is an effector rather than a neural control centre.

phy-cns-460.why: Shivering rapidly increases heat production through involuntary contractions of skeletal muscle. The resulting ATP turnover and metabolism can raise heat production substantially above the resting level.

notes.A: Parasympathetic activation is not the usual effector responsible for a large acute rise in thermogenesis during cold exposure.
notes.B: Thyroid hormone can increase metabolic rate over longer periods. Shivering provides a more immediate large increase in cold conditions.
notes.D: Radiation transfers heat between the body and its surroundings. It does not create metabolic heat within the body.
notes.E: Reduced sympathetic constrictor tone can increase skin blood flow and favour heat loss rather than heat production.

phy-cns-461.why: Eccrine sweat glands are activated by sympathetic postganglionic fibres that release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. This cholinergic pattern is unusual because many other sympathetic effectors use noradrenaline.

notes.A: Brown adipose thermogenesis is driven largely by sympathetic noradrenergic signals acting on adipocyte adrenergic receptors.
notes.B: Cold vasoconstriction in the hand chiefly involves sympathetic adrenergic activity and is distinct from cholinergic sweat secretion.
notes.C: Shivering is produced by patterned activation of skeletal muscle through somatic motor pathways.
notes.E: Behavioural changes such as seeking warmth involve central processing and voluntary action rather than direct sweat-gland innervation.

phy-cns-462.why: Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature through changes in heat production, heat transfer and behaviour. It helps maintain internal temperature within a range compatible with normal function.

notes.A: Osmoregulation maintains effective solute concentration and water balance. It is distinct from the control of temperature.
notes.B: Thermodynamics concerns energy and heat in physical systems. It is not the name of the physiological temperature control process.
notes.D: Regulation is a general term and does not specify which physiological variable is controlled.
notes.E: Homeostasis is the broader maintenance of a stable internal environment. Thermoregulation is one part of it.

phy-cns-463.why: As sweat evaporates, it takes heat from the skin. This helps cool the body, especially when radiation and convection are limited by a warm environment.

notes.B: Sweat contains sodium and chloride, but removing excess salt is not its main function. The kidneys handle most long-term salt balance.
notes.C: Water in sweat is the medium that evaporates to cool the body. It is not a principal route for regulating excess body water.
notes.D: Sweat may contain small amounts of urea. The kidneys provide the main route for urinary urea excretion.
notes.E: Bilirubin is processed by the liver and excreted in bile. Sweat is not a major route of bilirubin elimination.

phy-cns-464.why: When body temperature rises, thermoregulatory pathways increase cutaneous blood flow. More heat reaches the skin, where it can be lost to cooler surroundings or with evaporation of sweat.

notes.A: Sweat production normally rises with a thermal load, increasing the potential for evaporative heat loss.
notes.C: Cutaneous vasoconstriction reduces heat transfer to the surface. It is a cold-defence response.
notes.D: Piloerection can help trap an insulating air layer in fur-bearing animals and is associated with cold rather than heat defence.
notes.E: Shivering increases skeletal muscle heat production during cooling and is normally suppressed by warming.

phy-cns-465.why: Cooling suppresses eccrine sweat gland secretion by reducing thermoregulatory sudomotor drive. This conserves heat without requiring contraction of a skeletal or vascular smooth muscle effector.

notes.A: Cutaneous vasoconstriction decreases the vessel lumen through contraction of vascular smooth muscle.
notes.B: Hairs rise when arrector pili smooth muscle contracts, although the insulating effect in humans is small.
notes.C: Shivering depends on involuntary contractions of skeletal muscle that increase metabolic heat production.
notes.E: Increased ventilation requires respiratory muscle activity. It is not the standard heat-conserving response to mild cooling.

phy-cns-466.why: Warming reduces the need for cutaneous vasoconstriction and can activate cutaneous vasodilator pathways. Surface arterioles widen, increasing blood flow and transferring more heat from the core to the skin.

notes.A: Blood vessels transport oxygen, but absorbing oxygen from adjacent tissue is not their thermoregulatory response to warming.
notes.C: The arterioles remain in their anatomical positions. They regulate skin perfusion by changing calibre.
notes.D: The thermoregulatory response involves a change in vascular tone and blood flow rather than uptake of tissue water.
notes.E: Constriction decreases skin blood flow and helps conserve heat in the cold.

phy-cns-467.why: Parietal somatosensory cortices help localise a painful stimulus and discriminate its sensory features. Pain experience also involves other regions, including the insular and cingulate cortices.

notes.B: Primary auditory perception depends on the superior temporal cortex. Frontal areas can influence attention and interpretation but are not primary auditory cortex.
notes.C: The occipital lobes contain primary visual cortex, so occipital damage chiefly causes visual deficits.
notes.D: Language comprehension depends mainly on dominant-hemisphere temporal and temporoparietal networks. Right parietal cortex is more associated with spatial attention and related functions.
notes.E: This pairing includes a correct somatosensory role but misplaces primary auditory perception in the frontal lobe.

phy-cns-468.why: Broca aphasia typically causes effortful, nonfluent speech with short or grammatically simplified phrases. It follows injury to the dominant frontal language network. Comprehension is often relatively better preserved than speech production.

notes.A: Most left-handed people still have left-hemisphere language dominance, although right-sided or bilateral representation is more common than among right-handers.
notes.C: Language is usually left-dominant in right-handed people. Right-sided dominance is uncommon.
notes.D: Broca aphasia is a language-production disorder. Weakness of lips or tongue can occur with nearby motor injury but is not required.
notes.E: Wernicke aphasia involves the dominant posterior temporal language network and is characterised by fluent speech with impaired comprehension.
